sentences.text: The genus name blends the local Mistral wind with Azhdarcho, the type genus of its family.
The species epithet recognizes Jean-Pierre Maggi, the mayor of Velaux, for backing the excavation project.
A distinctive feature is a raised bump on the lower jaw midline, found 18 centimeters from the tip, a trait shared with Alanqa.
The upper jaw surface displays blunt, raised ridges along the edges, while the joint itself forms a V-shape without a lower ridge.
Another potential characteristic is a gentle curve at the jaw tip, and the upper arm bone is only sixty-six percent the length of the forearm bone.
This creature holds the distinction of being the first pterosaur named from the Late Cretaceous of Western Europe.
While the specific specimen measured between 4.24 and 4.85 meters across, adults likely reached five to six meters in span.
The holotype, a partial skeleton including part of the lower jaw, was found on a five-square-meter patch within a larger layer.
Xavier Valentin discovered the site in 1992, and the species was formally described in 2018 by Valentin, Vullo, Garcia, Godefroit, and Cincotta.
The upper arm bone measured nineteen centimeters, leading to estimates of nearly 4.5 meters using formulas from Averianov or extrapolations from Zhejiangopterus.
Multiple calculations support the hypothesis that this individual had a wingspan of approximately 4.5 meters.
It belongs to the family Azhdarchidae, though the original 2018 description lacked a detailed cladistic analysis.
Research places it in either subfamily Azhdarchinae or Quetzalcoatlinae, with a 2021 study by Brian Andres suggesting a sister relationship to Aerotitan.
This animal lived during the Campanian and Maastrichtian ages of the Late Cretaceous, specifically from 83.6 to 72.2 million years ago.
Scientists disagree on its exact evolutionary position, as its phylogenetic placement changes depending on the study used.
